unit.title: HTTP and REST APIs
unit.description: Requests and responses, methods, status codes, headers, JSON bodies, REST resources, idempotency, API keys and bearer tokens, CORS, 429, pagination, webhooks

cards.definition: A request has a method, a URL, headers and sometimes a body. The response has a status code, headers and a body. Every API call, page load and image is one of these exchanges.
cards.example: POST /api/leads with a JSON body; the server answers 201 Created with the new lead.

cards.definition: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part of a resource, DELETE removes. GET must never change data.
cards.example: GET /orders lists orders; PATCH /orders/42 updates the status of order 42.

cards.definition: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx redirection, 4xx client error (400 bad request, 401 not authenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 422 invalid data, 429 too many requests), 5xx server error.
cards.example: A form with an invalid email gets 422; the API being down gets 503.

cards.definition: A style of API built around resources named by URLs (/customers, /customers/42) and manipulated with the HTTP methods, usually in JSON, with no session state kept on the server between requests.
cards.example: GET /customers/42/orders lists the orders of customer 42.

cards.definition: An operation that gives the same result whether it runs once or several times. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, which is why a double click can create two orders.
cards.example: Payment APIs accept an idempotency key so a retried POST does not charge twice.

cards.definition: APIs identify callers with a key or a token sent in a header, usually Authorization: Bearer <token>. Keys are secrets: they stay on the server, never in front-end code or in a URL.
A browser rule: a page can only read responses from another origin if that server allows it with Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. It protects users; servers and scripts are not limited by it.
cards.example: Your front end on app.example.com calls api.example.com: the API must allow that origin.

cards.definition: APIs return large lists page by page (page and limit, or a cursor) and limit how many calls you can make; over the limit they answer 429, often with a Retry-After header.
cards.example: Fetching 10,000 contacts 100 at a time, waiting when a 429 arrives.

exercises.prompt: Which method should create a new lead?
choices: POST
GET
DELETE
HEAD
exercises.explain: POST creates. GET only reads and must never change data, because browsers, crawlers and caches call it freely.

exercises.prompt: The API answers 401. What does it mean?
choices: You are not authenticated: missing or invalid credentials
The resource does not exist on the server
The server crashed while handling it
The request worked and returned nothing
exercises.explain: 401 means who are you? 403 means I know you, but you may not do this.

exercises.prompt: A form sends an email without @. Which status should a good API return?
exercises.explain: 422 (or 400) tells the client its data is invalid, ideally with a message per field. 500 would blame the server.

exercises.prompt: Which URL follows REST conventions to get the orders of customer 42?
choices: GET /customers/42/orders
GET /getOrdersOfCustomer?id=42
POST /customers/orders/get/42
GET /orders.php?action=list&c=42
exercises.explain: REST names resources with nouns and nests them; the method carries the action.

exercises.prompt: Sending the same POST twice can create two orders, while sending the same PUT twice leaves the same result.
exercises.explain: True. PUT is idempotent, POST is not. Payment APIs accept idempotency keys to make retries safe.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print when the API answers 404?
choices: HTTP 404
ok
A TypeError: Failed to fetch
undefined
exercises.explain: fetch only rejects on network errors. A 404 is a valid response: you must check response.ok yourself.

exercises.prompt: Where should an API key for a paid service be sent from?
choices: From your server, in an Authorization header
From the browser, in the URL query string
From the HTML, in a hidden input field
From a cookie readable by any script
exercises.explain: Anything sent from the browser can be read by users. Keys stay server-side; URLs end up in logs and history.

exercises.prompt: Your page on shop.example.com calls api.partner.com and the browser blocks the response with a CORS error. Who fixes it?
choices: The API server, by allowing your origin in its headers
You, by adding mode: "no-cors" and reading the body
Nobody: CORS errors are browser bugs
You, by retrying the request ten times
exercises.explain: CORS is decided by the server you call. Alternatively, call the API from your own server, where CORS does not apply.

exercises.prompt: The API answers 429 with Retry-After: 30. What should your script do?
choices: Wait 30 seconds, then retry
Retry at once in a tight loop
Switch to another API key at random
Stop and delete the data received
exercises.explain: 429 means too many requests. Respect Retry-After, and use exponential backoff when it is absent.

choices: A URL of yours that a service calls when an event happens
A library that hooks into the browser fetch
A cookie used to track API calls
A paid plan with more API calls
exercises.explain: Instead of polling Stripe every minute, you receive a POST on /webhooks/stripe when a payment succeeds. Verify its signature.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of calling an API from a server in order.
steps: Send the request with an Authorization header
Check response.ok and the status code
Handle the next page if a cursor is returned
exercises.explain: Credentials, request, status check, parsing, pagination. Skipping the status check is the most common bug.

exercises.prompt: Build the header line that sends a bearer token.
exercises.explain: Authorization: Bearer TOKEN is the standard form for OAuth access tokens and most API keys.
